messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 63

# The Weight of Walls

Tariq is a 41-year-old Lebanese-American construction worker who has spent the better part of two decades building things — framing houses, pouring foundations, raising structures that are meant to stand. There is something deliberate in that choice of work, though he has never quite put it into words. He grew up in a home where things fell apart.

He was seven years old the first time he saw his father hit his mother. He remembers the sound more than anything — the particular crack of a palm against a cheekbone, the way his mother's body folded against the kitchen counter. He stood in the hallway in his socks, frozen, holding a school permission slip he had wanted her to sign. He never handed it to her. He went back to his room, slid under his bed, and pressed his face into the carpet until the shouting stopped. This became a ritual that lasted eleven years. The hiding. The waiting. The listening for silence to know whether the silence was safe.

His father was not a monster in the way people imagine monsters. He worked, he prayed, he brought home groceries and sometimes laughed loudly at the dinner table. The violence arrived without announcement, and that unpredictability was its own kind of education. Tariq learned to read rooms before he entered them — the set of his father's jaw, the particular stillness that preceded an explosion. He became fluent in threat before he understood what threat meant.

He left home at eighteen, came to the United States with a cousin, and threw himself into physical labor with the kind of dedication that leaves little room for memory. For years, it worked well enough. He was good at his job, respected on job sites, known for showing up early and staying late. He didn't drink much, didn't cause trouble. He told himself he had left all of it behind in Beirut.

But the body keeps its own records. In his mid-thirties, the dreams started — vivid, suffocating replays in which he is always small and always watching. He wakes most mornings before four, heart hammering, the sheets damp, and he cannot return to sleep. He sits at his kitchen table in the dark and drinks coffee until it is time to go to work, because lying in bed feels unbearable, like being trapped.

On job sites, certain sounds reach inside him without warning. A foreman raising his voice at a subcontractor. The sudden clatter of scaffolding. A door slamming in a neighboring unit. His body responds before his mind can intervene — a flooding of adrenaline, a tightening in his chest that takes long minutes to subside. His coworkers notice that he startles easily and have learned not to approach him from behind. He laughs it off. He is skilled at laughing things off.

He has not been in a serious relationship. He has tried — there have been women he cared about — but he finds himself hypervigilant in domestic spaces in ways he cannot explain to a partner. The sound of raised voices in an apartment hallway can ruin an evening entirely. He becomes withdrawn, then apologetic, then distant until the relationship quietly dissolves. He tells himself he prefers solitude. He is not entirely sure he believes it.

What Tariq carries most heavily is a specific and corrosive shame — not for what was done to him, but for what he did not do. He was a child, and he hid. He knows, intellectually, that there was nothing else to do. But the seven-year-old in him has not accepted this, and at forty-one, Tariq still sometimes lies awake rehearsing the moment in the hallway, the permission slip in his hand, wondering what would have happened if he had simply walked into the kitchen and stood between them. He builds walls for a living. He has been building them inside himself for much longer.
